name: AI surface product lead
oneLine: Runs a chat or search surface (ChatGPT, Gemini, Copilot), increasingly with its own agent that shops on merchant sites; wants conversion, trust and clear liability.
goals: Let users complete a purchase from the conversation, with a checkout that finishes in one or two turns or that the surface's own agent completes on the merchant's site.
Get the surface's agent accepted on merchant websites without a per-merchant integration: signed requests at the edge and payment tokens that existing checkouts take.
Onboard many merchants through one protocol (ACP or UCP) instead of bespoke integrations.
Stay out of the merchant-of-record role: the merchant keeps orders, taxes, returns and compliance.
Prove to users and regulators that the agent bought what the user asked for and nothing else, with a record of each approval.
Carry a payment credential through checkout without ever holding raw card data.
Measure attribution: which recommendations led to orders, and what the platform earns from them.
pains: Instant Checkout's 2025 form was scaled back in March 2026. Since 2026-11-13, in a limited US rollout, OpenAI's own agent, a dot with a cloud browser, completes the merchant's existing checkout with a ChatGPT Wallet token, so the surface depends on sites not blocking its signed agent and on risk systems not declining agent orders.

Bot defenses and fraud models tuned against automation can block a legitimate agent or decline its orders even when it signs its requests (Web Bot Auth). Relaying user signals can help, but those signals raise their own questions: unregistered Forwarded parameters may not be covered by the signature, and they expose the user's IP address and location.

Visa's rules make the cardholder answer, within Visa's system, for an Agentic Payment Provider's actions, but Worldpay says no liability shift exists yet. The platform is still the most visible party to blame when a purchase goes wrong.
Each merchant supports a different subset of capabilities and payment handlers, so the checkout experience varies and negotiation adds latency.
Prompt injection on merchant pages and in product feeds can bias the agent, and users will hold the platform responsible.
Merchants object that platform checkout bypasses their pixels and customer data, and some have gone to court over agent access (Amazon v. Perplexity).
Governance of ACP and UCP sits with a few firms, one of which may be a direct competitor.
decisions: Which commerce protocol to adopt as primary, and whether to support both ACP and UCP.
Whether to host checkout inside the surface, hand off to the merchant with a continue_url, or let the surface's own agent complete the merchant's web checkout with a wallet token.
Which card networks, credential providers and PSPs supply payment tokens to the surface.
What user-intent proof (an AP2 mandate, Verifiable Intent, an approval record, or nothing beyond a scoped token) to require before a payment.
Which signals to send merchants and risk providers (a signed agent identity, user signals in a Forwarded header) and how much user data they expose.

How to keep ads separate from answers and disclose sponsored or affiliate results inside agent recommendations. In the EU, the Digital Fairness Act proposal of 2026-11-11 (not law) would make a business that offers consumers an agent that concludes contracts for them disclose any payment it receives for proposing a contract and then require the consumer to confirm that purchase.
